lead: A steam power plant runs on the Rankine cycle: a pump pushes water into a boiler, the boiler turns it into superheated steam, the steam expands through a turbine, and a condenser turns the exhaust back into water. The working fluid changes phase, so its properties come from steam tables, not from pv = RT. The Rankine cycle is the ideal model of every coal, nuclear and solar-thermal steam plant. This chapter fixes the four states, computes the work, heat, efficiency and steam rate, and shows how boiler pressure, steam temperature and condenser pressure change the result.
prereq: You need steam tables and the dryness fraction from the topics Steam tables and Mollier chart and Formation of steam, latent heat and dryness fraction, and the steady flow energy equation from the topic Steady flow energy equation and its applications.

blocks.text: Take state 1 as the turbine inlet. The four steady-flow processes are 1→2 isentropic expansion in the turbine, 2→3 condensation at constant pressure to saturated liquid, 3→4 isentropic pumping to boiler pressure, and 4→1 heating at constant pressure in the boiler (water heating, boiling and superheating). Each device obeys the steady flow energy equation with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, so every work and heat is an enthalpy difference, in kJ/kg of steam:

items: turbine work w<sub>T</sub> = h₁ − h₂; pump work w<sub>P</sub> = h₄ − h₃ = v<sub>f</sub>(p₁ − p₂), with v<sub>f</sub> in m³/kg and p in kPa;
heat added q<sub>in</sub> = h₁ − h₄; heat rejected q<sub>out</sub> = h₂ − h₃;
ηRankine = (wT − wP)/qin; specific steam consumption SSC = 3600/wnet in kg/kWh.

blocks.text: To find h₂, use s₂ = s₁. If s₁ is less than s<sub>g</sub> at the condenser pressure, the exhaust is wet with dryness x₂ = (s₁ − s<sub>f</sub>)/s<sub>fg</sub> and h₂ = h<sub>f</sub> + x₂h<sub>fg</sub>. If s₁ is greater than s<sub>g</sub>, the exhaust is still superheated and h₂ comes from the superheat table. The pump work is tiny, often below 1% of the turbine work, because liquid water hardly changes volume.

Why not a Carnot cycle with steam? It would need a pump to compress a wet mixture up to saturated liquid, which a pump cannot do, and the turbine would expand very wet steam. The Rankine cycle condenses completely, so it pumps liquid only, and superheating keeps the turbine exhaust drier. The price is that part of the heat enters at low temperature, while the feedwater warms up in the boiler.

The efficiency follows the mean temperature of heat addition, T<sub>m</sub> = q<sub>in</sub>/(s₁ − s₄), and the condenser temperature: η = 1 − T<sub>condenser</sub>/T<sub>m</sub>, with both in kelvin. Each change below moves one of them. Values are for the worked example's plant (40 bar, 400 °C, 0.1 bar), changing one thing at a time.

items: Higher boiler pressure raises the boiling temperature, so Tm rises and η rises. But the expansion line moves left on the T-s diagram and the exhaust gets wetter, which erodes the last turbine blades.
Higher superheat raises Tm and also dries the exhaust, so it helps on both counts; the limit is the creep strength of the superheater tubes and turbine inlet.

Lower condenser pressure lowers the temperature of heat rejection. Heat input rises slightly, the turbine work rises more, so η rises; the exhaust gets a little wetter and the condenser needs a good vacuum and cold cooling water.

blocks.text: Plants combine high pressure with high superheat, and reheat (next chapter) to keep the exhaust dryness above about 0.88 to 0.90.

A real turbine and pump have friction, so entropy rises. Their isentropic efficiencies are η<sub>T</sub> = (h₁ − h₂')/(h₁ − h₂) and η<sub>P</sub> = (h₄ − h₃)/(h₄' − h₃), where the primed states are the actual ones. With η<sub>T</sub> = 0.85 in the worked example's plant, h₂' = 3214.5 − 0.85 × 1070.0 = 2305.0 kJ/kg, the exhaust dryness becomes 0.883 and the cycle efficiency falls from 35.3% to 30.0%. Pressure drops in the boiler and pipes and heat loss lower it further.

examples.question: Steam enters the turbine of an ideal Rankine cycle at 40 bar and 400 °C and the condenser pressure is 0.1 bar. Find the dryness at the turbine exit, the turbine and pump work, the heat added, the cycle efficiency and the specific steam consumption. Compare the efficiency with a Carnot cycle between the same extreme temperatures.
steps: Steam tables at 40 bar, 400 °C (superheated): h₁ = 3214.5 kJ/kg, s₁ = 6.7714 kJ/kg·K.

At 0.1 bar (T<sub>sat</sub> = 45.81 °C): h<sub>f</sub> = 191.81, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2392.1 kJ/kg; s<sub>f</sub> = 0.6492, s<sub>fg</sub> = 7.4996, s<sub>g</sub> = 8.1488 kJ/kg·K; v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001010 m³/kg.
h₃ = h<sub>f</sub> = 191.81 kJ/kg. w<sub>P</sub> = 0.001010 × (4000 − 10) = 4.03 kJ/kg (pressures in kPa); h₄ = 195.84 kJ/kg.

Carnot between 673.15 K and 318.96 K: 1 − 318.96/673.15 = 0.526. The Rankine cycle is lower because its mean temperature of heat addition is only q<sub>in</sub>/(s₁ − s₄) = 3018.7/(6.7714 − 0.6492) = 493 K (s₄ = s₃ = s<sub>f</sub>), and 1 − 318.96/493 = 0.353.
examples.answer: x₂ = 0.816, w<sub>T</sub> = 1070.0 kJ/kg, w<sub>P</sub> = 4.03 kJ/kg, q<sub>in</sub> = 3018.7 kJ/kg, η = 35.3%, SSC = 3.38 kg/kWh; Carnot 52.6%.

traps: Pump work needs pressures in kPa: v<sub>f</sub>Δp = 0.001010 × 3990 = 4.03 kJ/kg. Putting in bar (39.9) gives 0.0403 kJ/kg, one hundred times too small, because 1 bar = 100 kPa.
Check that the exhaust is wet before using x₂ = (s₁ − s<sub>f</sub>)/s<sub>fg</sub>. If s₁ is above s<sub>g</sub> at the condenser pressure, the formula gives x > 1 and the steam is superheated.
Heat added is h₁ − h₄ (from pump exit), not h₁ − h₃. Leaving out the pump work here changes the answer only slightly, but examiners mark it.
Specific steam consumption is 3600/w<sub>net</sub> in kg/kWh, with w<sub>net</sub> in kJ/kg. Using w<sub>T</sub> instead of w<sub>net</sub> is a common slip.
Higher boiler pressure at the same temperature raises η but makes the exhaust wetter. Do not say it improves everything.

quiz.q: Name the four components of a simple steam power plant and the process in each.
quiz.a: Pump: isentropic compression of liquid (3→4). Boiler: constant-pressure heating (4→1). Turbine: isentropic expansion (1→2). Condenser: constant-pressure heat rejection to saturated liquid (2→3).

quiz.q: Why is the Rankine cycle used instead of the Carnot cycle in steam plants?
quiz.a: The Carnot cycle would need a pump to compress a wet mixture, which is impractical, and its turbine would handle very wet steam. The Rankine cycle condenses fully, so only liquid is pumped, and superheat keeps the turbine exhaust drier.

quiz.q: How does lowering the condenser pressure change the heat input, the work and the efficiency?
quiz.a: Heat input rises slightly (the condensate is colder), turbine work rises more (a longer expansion), and heat rejection falls, so the efficiency rises. In the table η goes from 35.3% at 0.1 bar to 37.3% at 0.05 bar.

quiz.q: A Rankine cycle gives w<sub>T</sub> = 950 kJ/kg and w<sub>P</sub> = 8 kJ/kg. Find the specific steam consumption.
In the worked example the plant must give 50 MW net. Find the steam flow rate.
Why does raising the boiler pressure at a fixed steam temperature make the turbine exhaust wetter?
quiz.a: At a higher pressure and the same temperature the steam has a lower entropy s₁. The isentropic expansion keeps s₂ = s₁, so the exhaust point lies further left inside the dome, at a lower dryness (0.864 at 20 bar, 0.724 at 120 bar).

quiz.q: With a turbine efficiency of 0.85 the cycle efficiency falls from 35.3% to 30.0%. Explain why a 15% turbine loss gives a much smaller relative fall in cycle efficiency than you might expect, but still a large absolute one.
quiz.a: The turbine loss reduces w<sub>net</sub> by 0.15 × 1070.0 = 160.5 kJ/kg, from 1066.0 to 905.5 kJ/kg, while q<sub>in</sub> stays 3018.7 kJ/kg. So η falls by 160.5/3018.7 = 5.3 percentage points, a 15% relative fall; the lost work leaves as extra heat in the condenser.

beyond: Large modern coal plants run supercritical or ultra-supercritical: above the critical pressure of water (about 221 bar) there is no boiling, and steam temperatures near 600 °C push efficiency past 40%. Solar-thermal and geothermal plants run Rankine cycles at low temperatures, sometimes with organic working fluids instead of water (the organic Rankine cycle). Search for "ultra-supercritical boiler", "organic Rankine cycle" and "combined cycle power plant".

figure.caption: The worked example’s Rankine cycle on the T-s diagram of water. Heat goes in along the 40 bar line (water heating, boiling at 250.4 °C, superheating to 400 °C), the turbine expands the steam straight down into the dome to dryness 0.816, and the condenser closes the cycle at 45.8 °C. Points 3 and 4 nearly coincide because the pump work is only 4.03 kJ/kg.
